title: Effects of Resistance Spot Welding HAZ Thermal Cycles on a Third-Generation Quenching and Partitioning Steel: An Integrated Approach via Physical Simulation and Industrial Welding Validation
abstract: Abstract Resistance spot welding (RSW) is the predominant joining technique in automotive body-in-white manufacturing, and the severe thermal cycles imposed during welding significantly influence the microstructure and mechanical behavior of advanced high-strength steels. In this work, the response of a third-generation quenching and partitioning steel grade QP1180 to representative RSW heat-affected zone (HAZ) thermal cycles was investigated through an integrated approach combining physical simulation with conventional RSW experiments.  Representative thermal cycles of the upper-critical (UCHAZ), intercritical (ICHAZ), and sub-critical (SCHAZ) regions were reproduced using physical simulation approach with a Gleeble® thermomechanical simulator. To achieve the extremely high heating and cooling rates characteristic of RSW, a dedicated notched specimen geometry was designed and optimized via a transient thermo-electrical finite element model. The optimized geometry was subsequently validated experimentally, confirming the accurate reproduction of the target RSW thermal cycles in the physical simulation tests. Microstructural evolution was characterized by light optical and scanning electron microscopy, and the local mechanical response was evaluated through microhardness measurements correlated with peak temperature. To relate local HAZ behavior to structural performance, resistance spot-welded joints were produced under industrial conditions consistent with the simulated thermal cycles and mechanically tested by shear tensile and cross-tensile configurations. In addition, metallographic and hardness analyses were performed on real welded joints for comparison with the simulated results, although the inherent complexity of the welding process limits a direct point-by-point correlation between local thermal history and resulting properties, which can instead be effectively achieved through physical simulation.  The results establish a direct processing–microstructure–property–performance relationship for resistance spot-welded QP1180 steel and highlight the engineering relevance of the hardness–peak temperature correlation for interpreting welding thermal history and joint performance, while demonstrating the capability of the proposed physical simulation approach to support and enhance the interpretation of experimental observations on real welded joints.
journal: Journal of Materials Engineering and Performance

sections.heading: Introduction
paragraphs: Lightweight body-in-white (BIW) design combined with improved crash performance is a key challenge for the modern automotive industry (Ref  1 ). To meet these requirements, the use of advanced high-strength steels (AHSS) has significantly increased, enabling weight reduction while maintaining structural integrity and safety (Ref  2 ). Among these, press-hardened steels (PHS) are widely used for structural automotive components due to their high strength and thickness reduction potential (Ref  3 ,  4 - 5 ).

Achieving such high strength requires hot forming through the press-hardening process, which involves heating the blank to the fully austenitic temperature followed by forming and die quenching to obtain a fully martensitic microstructure at room temperature (Ref  6 ,  7 - 8 ). However, this process is energy-intensive, prompting the development of alternative high-strength material solutions (Ref  9 ).

For this reason, steelmakers have increasingly focused on third-generation AHSS, which aim to combine high strength and ductility with improved processing efficiency and reduced energy demand (Ref  10 ,  11 ). Among these, quenching and partitioning (Q&P) steels are considered key candidates due to their excellent strength–ductility balance. Their microstructure typically consists of martensite and retained austenite, and in some grades, also ferrite (Ref  12 ,  13 ,  14 - 15 ). As a result, Q&P sheet steels, including grades such as QP980 and QP1180, are gaining relevance in automotive structural applications (Ref  12 ).

Since automotive BIW manufacturing relies extensively on welding, joining processes inevitably influence the final performance of AHSS components (Ref  16 ,  17 ). Resistance spot welding (RSW) is the predominant joining method in the automotive sector, with each vehicle containing several thousand spot welds. However, the severe thermal cycles imposed during RSW significantly alter the designed microstructure of AHSS, particularly within the heat-affected zone (HAZ), potentially leading to local softening and reduced joint performance (Ref  18 ,  19 ,  20 - 21 ).

Several studies have investigated the microstructural evolution and hardness distribution in resistance spot-welded Q&P steels. However, most available works focus primarily on post-weld characterization of real joints, while a systematic correlation between the imposed RSW thermal cycles, the resulting local microstructural transformations, and the associated mechanical response remains limited.

In this context, physical simulation using thermomechanical simulators represents a powerful approach, as it enables controlled reproduction of welding thermal cycles and isolation of the effects of peak temperature, heating rate, and cooling rate on microstructural evolution. Unlike conventional post-weld analyses, this method allows a point-by-point investigation of material behavior across the heat-affected zone under well-defined thermal conditions.

Therefore, in this work, thermal cycles representative of RSW HAZ regions were reproduced using a Gleeble thermomechanical simulator. A dedicated specimen geometry, optimized through finite element analysis, was developed to enable accurate reproduction of the extremely rapid heating and cooling cycles characteristic of RSW. Microstructural characterization and local hardness measurements were then performed to establish correlations between thermal history, microstructure, and mechanical response.

In parallel, resistance spot-welded QP1180 joints were produced under industrial welding conditions consistent with the simulated thermal histories and characterized in terms of mechanical behavior, microstructure and hardness to provide a conventional experimental reference for comparison with the physical simulation results.

sections.heading: Material
paragraphs: The material investigated in this study is a Quenching and Partitioning (Q&P) steel of grade QP1180 a 1.2-mm-thick galvanized sheet. The sheet exhibits the typical multiphase microstructure of Q&P steels, consisting of tempered martensite, appearing dark gray in the scanning electron microscopy (SEM) image reported in Fig.  1 (a) and a mixture of fresh martensite and retained austenite, not clearly distinguishable in the reported image and appearing light gray. The appearance of the material microstructure, in light optical microscopy (LOM), is instead reported in Fig.  1 (b), where details are not distinguished due to the small scale. Fig. 1 Microstructure of the QP1180 steel in the as-received condition (a) SEM micrograph acquired using a secondary electron detector (SED mode) with 15 kV accelerating voltage; (b) optical micrograph. Details on metallographic preparation and instruments used are identical to those used to investigate the samples post-weld and are described in the next section

The carbon content reported in the literature for this steel grade is approximately 0.20 wt.% (Ref  22 ,  23 - 24 ). The Mn and Si contents were measured by EDS using a JEOL JCM-7000 SEM equipped with an EDS detector and were found to be 2.91 wt.% Mn and 1.67 wt.% Si, consistent with the literature values (Ref  22 ,  23 - 24 ).

Mechanical characterization in the as-received condition was carried out through standard tensile tests, as reported in a previous study by the authors (Ref  25 ). The material exhibited an ultimate tensile strength of 1196 ± 14 MPa, a yield strength of 1004 ± 30 MPa, and an elongation at break of 11.7 ± 1.8%. These results are in good agreement with previously published data (Ref  22 ,  24 ).

sections.heading: Physical Simulation
paragraphs: The objective of this study was to investigate the mechanical and microstructural variations that develop throughout the entire heat-affected zone (HAZ) generated during a resistance spot welding (RSW) process, through a combined approach integrating controlled physical simulation and conventional welding experiments.

Gleeble®3180 physical simulator was employed to reproduce at laboratory scale the thermal cycles characteristic of different HAZ sub-regions: UCHAZ (Upper Critical Heat-Affected Zone, T > A 3 ), ICHAZ (Intercritical Heat-Affected Zone, A 1  < T < A 3 ), and SCHAZ (Sub-Critical Heat-Affected Zone, T < A 1 ), thus enabling a controlled, point-by-point correlation between the imposed thermal history and the resulting microstructural and mechanical properties.

The thermal cycles representative of different HAZ sub-regions, reproduced using the Gleeble simulator, are shown in Fig.  1 . These cycles were derived from the literature data, where they were experimentally measured by high-speed thermography during resistance spot welding of a PHS1500 steel (Ref  26 ) and were adopted in this study as a reference to accurately replicate industrial RSW conditions. As observed in Fig.  2 , these cycles are extremely severe, featuring very high heating rates (from 1300 to 6000 °C/s) and cooling rates (from 600 to 3000 °C/s). Fig. 2 Reference thermal cycles for UCHAZ, ICHAZ, and SCHAZ during RSW

Since the aim of this work is to faithfully reproduce these cycles using the Gleeble simulator, in order to analyze the mechanical and microstructural responses under controlled conditions, careful test design was required. The Gleeble is capable of reaching heating rates up to 8000 °C/s (Ref  27 ); therefore, the heating stage did not pose significant challenges. The specimens are heated by Joule effect: a control thermocouple welded at the specimen center measures the temperature, compares it with the target value, and allows the PID system to modulate the current density accordingly.

During testing, the specimens are clamped between water-cooled jaws, which generates a thermal gradient with the peak temperature at the control point and decreasing values toward the ends. Consequently, cooling occurs mainly through conduction toward the cold regions. In order to reproduce the high cooling rates required by the reference cycles, the specimen geometry had to be optimized. Specifically, the central cross section was reduced to increase the amount of surrounding cold material and thus enhance heat extraction.

Specimen design was supported by a transient 3D thermo-electrical finite element model developed in COMSOL Multiphysics to replicate the Gleeble test and identify the geometry capable of achieving the desired cooling rates. The FE model, previously described in Palmieri et al. (Ref  28 ), was updated with a modified geometry and with temperature-dependent thermophysical properties representative of QP1180 steel, derived from the literature data (Ref  29 ). The configuration used for parametric study is shown in Fig.  3 . The parameters varied were D and w, corresponding to the length and width of the notched region. D was varied between 2 and 5 mm, while w was varied between 1 and 2 mm. Fig. 3 Notched specimen geometry adopted for Gleeble tests, highlighting the variable parameters D and w

Once the optimal geometry was defined, the specimens were tested on the Gleeble simulator. Type K thermocouples were used: one at the center (control thermocouple) and two positioned at distances determined by the selected geometry to monitor the thermal gradient.

After the physical simulation tests, the specimens were prepared metallographically by grinding with SiC papers, polishing using diamond suspensions from 9 µm down to 1 µm, and etching with 2% Nital. Microstructural observations were performed using both a benchtop scanning electron microscope (Jeol JCM-7000), equipped with a tungsten thermionic electron source and an optical microscope (Nikon Optiphot 2) equipped with DA-Fi3 microscope camera, in the region where the control thermocouple was welded. SEM images were acquired under constant operating conditions (accelerating voltage of 15 kV and secondary electron imaging mode).

Microhardness measurements were performed to establish a local correlation between hardness and the peak temperature experienced during the thermal cycle. The position of the welded control thermocouple was used as the reference point (zero position) for the measurements. Indentations were performed symmetrically on both sides of this location along the longitudinal axis, corresponding to the direction of the thermal gradient, up to a distance of ± 3 mm, with a spacing of 0.15 mm between adjacent indents. The tests were conducted using a Struers Duravista 40 microhardness tester under an applied load of 0.1 kgf.

No macroscopic mechanical testing was performed on the physically simulated specimens. This choice is motivated by the extremely reduced cross-sectional dimensions of the notched region, which would lead to severe stress concentration effects, unstable deformation behavior, and poor reproducibility of mechanical results. Under such conditions, the measured response would not be representative of the intrinsic material behavior associated with the simulated thermal cycle.

sections.heading: Industrial Welds
paragraphs: To validate the proposed physical simulation methodology and provide a direct comparison with real welding conditions, resistance spot-welded joints were produced by welding two QP1180 sheets (50 mm × 50 mm, 1.2 mm thickness each) under industrial welding parameters consistent with the physically simulated thermal histories. Resistance spot welding tests were carried out in accordance with the SEP 1220 international standard. Welding experiments were performed using a MF/DC pedestal spot welding machine equipped with water-cooled, tip-dressed Cu-based electrodes (F1-16 type, Ø 8 mm).

The electrode force was set to 4000 N, with a welding time of 300 ms and squeeze/holding times of 1000 ms. The weldability lobe was systematically investigated by varying the welding current, while all other process parameters were kept constant, in order to identify the minimum and maximum current levels capable of producing compliant spot-welded joints.

The welded joints were then sectioned through the weld center, mounted, and metallographically prepared following the same procedure adopted for the Gleeble specimens (grinding, polishing, and etching with 2% Nital). Nugget dimensions were measured on the resulting metallographic cross sections and used to assess weld quality. Microstructural characterization was performed using optical microscopy and scanning electron microscopy as described above.

Microhardness measurements were carried out across the weld cross section, following the scheme illustrated in Fig.  4 . Indentations were performed using a Shimadzu HMV-G microhardness tester, equipped with a Vickers diamond indenter, with a spacing of 0.1 mm and an applied load of 0.1 kgf, in order to evaluate the local variation in hardness across different weld regions. Fig. 4 Scheme of microhardness measurements on the performed joint

sections.heading: Optimization of Specimen Geometry for Physical Simulation Tests
paragraphs: The parametric numerical study allowed assessing the influence of D and w on both the cooling rate and the thermal gradient. The results discussed below refer to one of the most critical thermal conditions in terms of cooling severity, namely the UCHAZ thermal cycle with a peak temperature of 1000 °C.

Figure  5 (a) shows the evolution of the cooling curve as a function of D, for w equal to 1 mm. Conversely, Fig.  5 (b) illustrates the cooling rate evaluated at 700 °C during cooling from the peak temperature (1000 °C), as a function of both parameters D and w. The cooling rate was assessed at 700 °C in line with previous resistance spot welding studies, where this temperature is commonly used as a reference to correlate cooling severity with austenite decomposition and martensitic transformation (Ref  30 ,  31 - 32 ). Fig. 5 Results of the numerical simulation of the thermal response of the optimized specimen geometry under simulated RSW conditions (a) Thermal cycles for various diameters; (b) Cooling rates (1000-700 °C) for D at w = 1 and 2 mm; (c) Comparison of target and reproduced cycles

As expected, a reduction in either D or w leads to a significant increase in cooling rate. Notably, the configuration D1w1 (D = 1 mm and w = 1 mm) enables cooling rates on the order of 3000 °C/s, which are representative of the most severe thermal conditions occurring in real resistance spot welding processes.

In Fig.  5 (c), the continuous line represents the target RSW thermal cycle within the UCHAZ region that the physical simulation aims to reproduce. The dashed line instead shows the thermal cycle measured by the control thermocouple during the test. The comparison confirms that an appropriate optimization of the specimen geometry enables a sufficiently accurate reproduction of the actual thermal cycles.

To further validate the numerical predictions, three thermocouples were welded onto the specimen used for physical simulation tests: one at the center, one approximately 0.8 mm from the center, and one at 3 mm from the center. Figure  6  presents a comparison between numerical and experimental results in terms of the thermal gradient across the specimen at the instant corresponding to the peak temperature. Fig. 6 Comparison between numerical and experimental thermal gradients across the specimen at the peak temperature
The observed agreement between simulations and measurements shown in Fig.  5 (c) supports the reliability of the optimized geometry.

sections.heading: Microstructural Analysis and Hardness Evolution
paragraphs: The microstructural evolution induced by the simulated RSW thermal cycles provides insight into the transformations occurring in various sub-regions of the HAZ. SEM and optical microscopy investigation presented in Fig.  7  reveal the progressive morphological changes as the maximum exposure temperature, peak temperature, during the thermal cycle varies. Fig. 7 SEM and optical microscopy images of the UCHAZ (CGHAZ–FGHAZ), ICHAZ, and SCHAZ produced by simulated RSW thermal cycles

In the UCHAZ subjected to a peak temperature of 1400 °C, coarse austenite grains are observed, containing well-defined martensitic packets composed of long, straight, and highly oriented blocks of martensite laths. This hierarchical structure is characteristic of martensitic transformation from heavily grown austenite grains, and represents the typical microstructure of the coarse-grained heat-affected zone (CGHAZ) in low-C, low alloyed steel (Ref  33 ).

In the UCHAZ exposed to a peak of 1000 °C, the microstructure consists of fine martensitic structure, where the hierarchical microstructure of lath martensite is not evident. Further details could be revealed by Electron Back Scattered Diffraction (EBSD) study, which is beyond the scope of the present work. The micrograph indicates that the transformation occurred from fine-grained austenite, typical of the fine-grained heat-affected zone (FGHAZ) (Ref  33 ).

At a peak temperature of 800 °C, partial austenitization takes place, i.e., the temperature lies in the intercritical region, eventually leading to a mixed microstructure representative of equilibrium conditions, hence composed of ferrite (F) and austenite. Upon rapid cooling, the austenite transforms into martensite (M), resulting in a ferrite–martensite microstructure. The corresponding image in Fig.  7  is interpreted consistently, where dark gray featureless areas are interpreted as ferrite, while martensite appears light gray. Small retained austenite regions may also be present within the martensite units, which cannot be resolved at the applied magnification.

Finally, at 450 °C, below the critical temperature Ac 1 , the temperature is sufficiently high to induce tempering of the fresh martensite regions present in the base material, but sufficiently low that no other changes in the microstructure are expected (450 °C is typically the partitioning temperature in Q&P steel (Ref  34 )). Consistently, in comparison with the SEM micrograph in Fig.  1 , the fraction of light gray area, representing fresh martensite and austenite, is reduced as consequence of disappearance of the fresh martensite regions.

The hardness values obtained after the simulated welding thermal cycles are reported in Fig.  8 . In particular, Fig.  8 (a) shows, as a representative example, the hardness profile as a function of the distance from the specimen center for the UCHAZ condition with a peak temperature of 1400 °C. This condition was selected because, due to the intrinsic thermal gradient imposed by the Gleeble system, the maximum peak temperature is reached at the specimen center and progressively decreases toward the grips, allowing a single specimen to span a wide range of peak temperatures. Consequently, the hardness profile along the specimen is representative of the behavior observed in all tested conditions. As described in section  3.1 , in fact, the FE model enables each spatial position to be associated with the corresponding local peak temperature, allowing the hardness to be expressed as a function of peak temperature rather than distance. For the UCHAZ-T1400 condition, this transformation would result in a hardness–peak temperature trend consistent with those reported in Fig.  8 (b). This figure summarizes the hardness as a function of peak temperature for all tested conditions. The individual curves show a significant overlap, indicating that they can be interpreted as a single, continuous hardness–peak temperature relationship over the investigated range. Fig. 8 (a) Hardness distribution as a function of the distance from the specimen center for the UCHAZ condition with a peak temperature of 1400 °C; (b) Hardness as a function of peak temperature for all tested conditions

The highest hardness values are measured in the UCHAZ, corresponding to peak temperatures between approximately 1400 and 1000 °C. In this region, the microstructure is predominantly martensitic due to complete austenitization followed by rapid cooling. Interestingly, the coarse-grained HAZ exhibits hardness values approximately 35 HV lower than those measured in the fine-grained region, which indicate that Hall–Petch effect plays a role in the present case.

The minimum hardness, approximately 350 HV0.1, was observed for peak temperatures in the range of 500-700 °C, corresponding to the SCHAZ region. This represents a softening of about 16% compared to the base material which is caused by the tempering of the fresh martensite structure while transiting in this temperature regime. Eventually, hardening restarts upon reaching 700 °C, which could indicate decomposition of retained austenite prior to restart of the re-austenitization process, which would lead to further hardening by developing condition for a new martensitic transformation upon subsequent cooling. These results are consistent with data reported in the literature (Ref  21 ), where microstructural and hardness analyses were performed directly on spot-welded joints rather than on specimens subjected to thermal cycles using a physical simulator. This agreement was further demonstrated with direct investigation of an actual weld. Results are reported below.

sections.heading: Experimental Validation on Resistance Spot Welded QP1180 Joints
paragraphs: The welding current range identified for QP1180 steel is reported in Fig.  9  together with the corresponding nugget diameters and observed failure modes. Fig. 9 Weldability window of QP1180 steel under resistance spot welding—relationship between welding current and nugget diameter
The welding current was progressively increased to identify the lower and upper bounds of the weldability window.

Despite these geometric differences, the weld nuggets remain macroscopically sound and free from defects such as solidification cracks or voids at both current levels. In addition, no macroscopic evidence of liquid metal embrittlement (LME) is observed in the analyzed cross sections, indicating a negligible susceptibility of the investigated galvanized QP1180 steel to LME under the adopted welding conditions (Table  1 ). Table 1 Mechanical properties of QP1180 steel investigated R m , MPa R p0.2 , MPa A, % 1196 1004 11.7
Evidently, the observed features correspond to those reported for the samples subjected to physical simulation tests.

Similarly, the hardness profile across the weld clearly reflects the profile obtained in Fig.  8 , in spite on a different length scale, which is direct result of the different sample geometry, with hardness evolving from 560 ± 10 HV0.1 in the UCHAZ, to a minimum of the 350 ± 10 HV0.1 in the SCHAZ and finally reaching the hardness of the base material at approximately 4 mm from the center of the joint. Furthermore, Fig.  12  provides information on the fusion zone of the joint. The fusion zone exhibits relatively uniform hardness values in the range of approximately 470 ± 10 HV0.1, which are slightly lower than those measured in the adjacent upper-critical heat-affected zone possibly as a consequence of further coarsening of the microstructure in this area, or alternatively to segregation-induced effects. Further investigation of this point is beyond the scope of the present manuscript.
Figure  13  shows the average shear tensile load–displacement curves obtained from three tests for each welding current condition.

Generally, the increase in shear strength with welding current is mainly associated with the enlargement of the weld nugget resulting from the higher heat input (Ref  35 ,  36 ). However, the difference in peak load remains relatively limited, and the overall shape of the load–displacement curves is similar across the investigated current range, indicating stable joint behavior and no significant macroscopic differences in shear response.

Figure  14  shows the cross-tensile load–displacement curves, reported as the average of three tests for each welding current condition. Peak forces range between 3 and 4 kN, significantly lower than those measured under shear loading, due to the high tensile stress concentration at the nugget edge.

sections.heading: Conclusions
paragraphs: In this study, the effects of resistance spot welding thermal cycles on the microstructural evolution and mechanical behavior of a third-generation quenching and partitioning steel grade QP1180 were investigated through a combined approach integrating physical simulation and experimental validation.

The main findings can be summarized as follows: Representative thermal cycles of different heat-affected zone sub-regions (UCHAZ, ICHAZ, and SCHAZ) were successfully reproduced using a Gleeble® thermomechanical simulator. The development and optimization of a dedicated notched specimen geometry, supported by a transient thermo-electrical finite element model, enabled the achievement of heating and cooling rates comparable to those occurring during industrial RSW processes. This approach allowed the isolated and controlled investigation of the influence of peak temperature and thermal history on local material behavior. Microstructural characterization coupled with hardness measurements revealed distinct phase transformations and associated mechanical response across the HAZ. Complete austenitization followed by rapid cooling led to coarse- and fine-grained strong martensitic microstructures in the UCHAZ, depending on the peak temperature. Partial austenitization in the ICHAZ resulted in heterogeneous ferrite–martensite microstructures with mid-hardness levels, while sub-critical thermal cycles caused tempering of the martensitic base microstructure, possibly coupled to austenite decomposition in the higher temperature regime in the SCHAZ, and minimum hardness values. Experimental resistance spot-welded joints showed strong qualitative and quantitative agreement with the Gleeble-based results in terms of microstructure and hardness distribution along the joint. This confirms that physical simulation is a reliable approach for reproducing and interpreting the local transformations occurring during real RSW processes. On this basis, the validated methodology can be applied to investigate different welding conditions at laboratory scale, enabling the prediction of joint behavior without performing multiple time- and cost-intensive welding trials in industrial environments. Moreover, this approach enables a straightforward point-by-point correlation between local thermal history and the resulting mechanical and microstructural properties.
